Paper: Song et al. (2020), [Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.13456), published at ICLR 2021.
The paper unifies several score-based and diffusion models through a forward stochastic differential equation and its reverse-time counterpart.
The learned object is the gradient of the noisy-data log-density at each time.

## Problem

For a differentiable density $p_t(x)$, its score is the vector

$$
  s_t(x)=\nabla_x\log p_t(x).
$$

It points locally toward increasing log-density and has the same dimension as $x$.
This is a derivative with respect to the sample, not a scalar quality score or a gradient with respect to network parameters.
For $p_\theta(x)=e^{-E_\theta(x)}/Z_\theta$, the normalising constant disappears under this derivative, giving $s_\theta(x)=-\nabla_x E_\theta(x)$. [Hyvärinen (2005), §2](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume6/hyvarinen05a/hyvarinen05a.pdf#page=2).
The [probability study](../../study-notes/machine-learning/energy-based-models.qmd#energy-and-score) develops the energy and sampling connection.

The data density and its score are unknown, so training needs an objective that can be estimated from examples.
Sampling additionally needs a procedure that converts the learned local directions into a distribution of complete outputs.

## Previous attempts

Classical score matching fits a model score by minimising its squared distance from the data score.
Integration by parts removes the unknown data score from the objective, under suitable differentiability, integrability, and boundary conditions.
For a model field $s_\theta$, the resulting trainable expression is

$$
  \mathbb E_{x\sim p}\left[
  \tfrac12\|s_\theta(x)\|^2
  +\nabla_x\cdot s_\theta(x)\right].
$$

The divergence is the sum of coordinate derivatives, $\sum_i\partial s_{\theta,i}/\partial x_i$.
The omitted term is independent of the model parameters. [Hyvärinen, Theorem 1](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume6/hyvarinen05a/hyvarinen05a.pdf#page=3).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: remove the unknown data score"}

Let $s=\nabla\log p$ and start from the Fisher-divergence objective

$$
  J=\tfrac12\mathbb E_p\|s_\theta-s\|^2.
$$

The cross term satisfies

$$
  \mathbb E_p[s_\theta\cdot s]
  =\int s_\theta(x)\cdot\nabla p(x)\,dx.
$$

If the boundary contribution vanishes, coordinatewise integration by parts gives

$$
  \int s_\theta\cdot\nabla p\,dx
  =-\int p\,\nabla\cdot s_\theta\,dx.
$$

Expanding the square therefore yields

$$
  J=\mathbb E_p\left[
  \tfrac12\|s_\theta\|^2+\nabla\cdot s_\theta
  \right]+C,
$$

where $C=\tfrac12\mathbb E_p\|s\|^2$ is independent of $\theta$.
The plus sign on the divergence comes from subtracting the cross term and then integrating it by parts.
The identity is not valid without the required boundary and regularity assumptions.

:::

Denoising score matching instead uses the known conditional score of an artificial corruption process.
Training over multiple noise scales helps define useful scores away from the original data manifold, while [DDPM](ddpm.qmd) provides a discrete Gaussian noising construction.
Song et al. express these approaches in a common continuous-time framework. [Paper, §§2–3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.13456#page=2).

## Proposed solution

In this note, forward time runs from data at $t=0$ toward noise at $t=T$.
For a scalar diffusion coefficient $g(t)$, define

$$
  dx=f(x,t)\,dt+g(t)\,dW_t.
$$

The drift $f$ determines systematic motion, and $dW_t$ is a Brownian increment with covariance $dt\,I$ in forward time.
The coefficient $g$ controls the instantaneous noise scale; $g^2$ controls its variance rate.
Under the reversal conditions used in the paper, the reverse-time SDE is

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  dx={}&[f(x,t)-g(t)^2s_t(x)]\,dt\\
  &+g(t)\,d\bar W_t.
  \end{aligned}
$$

This equation is integrated from $T$ down to $0$, so $dt$ is negative and $\bar W$ denotes reverse-time Brownian motion.
The displayed sign must be interpreted together with that time direction. [Paper, §§3.1–3.2, Eqs. (5)–(6)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.13456#page=4).

For Gaussian perturbations of the form $x_t=a_t x_0+\sigma_t\epsilon$, the conditional score is available exactly:

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  \nabla_{x_t}\log p(x_t\mid x_0)
  &=-\frac{x_t-a_t x_0}{\sigma_t^2}\\
  &=-\frac{\epsilon}{\sigma_t}.
  \end{aligned}
$$

A denoising objective regresses $s_\theta(x_t,t)$ against this target, with a chosen time weighting.
At the squared-error optimum, the network learns its conditional average given the noisy state, which is the marginal score $s_t(x_t)$. [Paper, §3.3, Eq. (7)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.13456#page=4).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: denoising, marginal scores, and a conditional mean"}

Let $r_t(x,x_0)=\nabla_x\log p_t(x\mid x_0)$ denote the known conditional score.
Differentiating the noisy marginal density under its integral gives

$$
  s_t(x)=\int r_t(x,x_0)
  \frac{p_t(x\mid x_0)p_0(x_0)}{p_t(x)}\,dx_0.
$$

The fraction is the posterior density of the clean example given the noisy state, so this integral equals $\mathbb E[r_t(x,x_0)\mid x]$.

For additive Gaussian noise $x=x_0+\sigma\epsilon$, substitution gives

$$
  s(x)=\frac{\mathbb E[x_0\mid x]-x}{\sigma^2}.
$$

Rearranging yields the Gaussian conditional-mean identity often called Tweedie's formula:

$$
  \mathbb E[x_0\mid x]=x+\sigma^2s(x).
$$

For the scaled corruption $x_t=a_t x_0+\sigma_t\epsilon$, the corresponding result is

$$
  a_t\mathbb E[x_0\mid x_t]
  =x_t+\sigma_t^2s_t(x_t).
$$

These are conditional means under the specified corruption model, not exact recovery of the particular clean example that happened to produce a noisy input.
The derivation requires differentiating the mixture density under the integral and uses the Gaussian conditional score above.

:::

## Variance-preserving and variance-exploding processes

The variance-preserving SDE associated with the continuous DDPM limit is

$$
  dx=-\tfrac12\beta(t)x\,dt+\sqrt{\beta(t)}\,dW_t.
$$

Writing $a_t=\exp[-\tfrac12\int_0^t\beta(s)\,ds]$, its conditional law has mean $a_t x_0$ and covariance $(1-a_t^2)I$.
If the initial marginal covariance is $I$, it remains $I$; the name does not assert that every arbitrary initial data covariance is unchanged.
The variance-exploding family has zero drift and increasing added covariance:

$$
  dx=g(t)\,dW_t,
  \qquad v_t=\int_0^t g(s)^2\,ds.
$$

Here $v_t$ is the added variance and $\sqrt{v_t}$ is its standard deviation. [Paper, §3.4 and Appendix B](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.13456#page=5).

## Two sampling routes

The reverse SDE produces stochastic trajectories, and predictor-corrector sampling combines a numerical prediction step with score-based corrections.
The corresponding probability-flow ODE is

$$
  \frac{dx}{dt}=f(x,t)-\tfrac12g(t)^2s_t(x).
$$

With exact scores and the relevant regularity assumptions, it shares the forward SDE's time-indexed marginal densities.
It does not share the same random trajectories or all joint distributions across time.
The ODE is deterministic for a fixed starting sample, while drawing a new terminal noise sample still produces a new output. [Paper, §§4.2–4.3, Eq. (13)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.13456#page=7).

## Evidence

The paper evaluates alternative SDEs, predictor-corrector samplers, probability-flow likelihoods, and conditional image generation.
The experiments demonstrate that a learned score can support several sampling procedures and inverse-problem constructions within the tested image settings. [Paper, §§4–5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.13456#page=5).

## Limitations

Finite neural approximations and numerical solvers introduce errors, so exact SDE–ODE marginal equivalence does not guarantee identical practical samples or scores.
Score estimation at very small noise levels can be difficult, and sampling still requires repeated field evaluations.
The simple reverse formulas above assume $g$ depends only on time; more general state-dependent diffusion requires the additional terms given in the paper's appendix.
